name: Wachau

climate.koppen_name: Cold, no dry season, warm summer

terms: Austrian quality wine from approved grape varieties, tested by the state before sale. Prädikatswein and DAC wines sit within it.
Districtus Austriae Controllatus, Austria's rules for regionally typical wines. The wine must show the typical character of its area.
keyfacts: Wachau has its own three-level classification, all for dry wines: Steinfeder up to 11.5% alcohol, Federspiel from 11.5 to 12.5%, and Smaragd with a minimum of 12.5%.
Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd wines are always white and dry, made without enrichment or added sugar and without any oak influence.
Vinea Wachau, the growers' association founded in 1983, began creating the Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd trademarks in 1984.
Vineyards climb steep Danube terraces built on dry stone walls, with soils of gneiss, amphibolite and wind-blown loess.
Riesling thrives on the shallow, poor terraces, while Grüner Veltliner does best in loess at the foot of slopes or in sandier soils near the Danube.

notes: Wines are rarely given new oak or malolactic, and are fuller bodied, closer to Alsace than to Germany.
The best Smaragd wines can age more than 20 years.

blurb.text: A wine region in Niederösterreich (Lower Austria), on the Danube west of Vienna, known for dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner. Its growers' association has its own three-level system for dry wines, from Steinfeder, up to 11.5 percent alcohol, to Smaragd. Grüner Veltliner covers 64 percent of vines.
